episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, July third, twenty-twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

The top story this week comes from the A.I. workforce front. A new study examining more than twenty-one thousand five hundred U.S. firms found that companies investing most heavily in A.I. grew their headcount by ten point two percent over a two-year period, according to research from financial technology company Ramp and workforce intelligence firm Revelio Labs, as reported by USA Today. The researchers divided firms into adoption tiers. Low-intensity adopters, spending an average of two dollars and seventy-eight cents per employee on A.I., saw little change in headcount. High-intensity adopters, spending an average of thirty-three dollars and sixty-seven cents per employee, grew headcount by ten point two percent, and entry-level headcount at those firms rose twelve percent, contradicting predictions that younger or less experienced workers face the greatest risk. The findings arrive amid public anxiety: fifty-three percent of Americans worry A.I. could cost them or someone in their household a job, according to a Reuters and Ipsos poll released in June. Ramp Economics Lab lead economist Ara Kharazian cautioned that the sample skews toward tech-forward companies and white-collar roles, excluding drivers and manufacturing workers, and that headcounts could still shift beyond the two-year window. The researchers stress the findings show correlation, not proof that A.I. spending causes hiring. Kharazian noted that most firms using A.I. do not see results immediately, with gains appearing only after sustained, high-intensity use. LinkedIn's head of economics for the Americas added that companies investing in new technology tend to have resources for labor as well, and that growing A.I. firms need human resources, marketing, and sales staff to support new opportunities.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation this week, four community colleges have been selected to design A.I.-ready work-based learning experiences through a new initiative backed by Google dot org, according to an announcement from the Education Design Lab. The AI Plus Durable Skills Work-Based Learning Design Challenge, launched in partnership with work-based learning platform Riipen, selected the Community College of Aurora in Colorado, Hudson County Community College in New Jersey, East Arkansas Community College, and Roxbury Community College in Boston. Each institution receives a ten-thousand-dollar implementation grant, access to Riipen's platform, and a facilitated design process led by the Lab. Pilot learning experiences launch in January twenty-twenty-seven and run through August twenty-twenty-seven, with students completing employer-designed projects reflecting real-world A.I. use cases. The Lab noted the colleges were selected for institutional readiness rather than interest in A.I. alone, and plans to publish an open-access library of tools, sample curricula, and best practices at the challenge's conclusion. The announcement cited research showing demand for A.I. literacy skills has grown more than seventy percent compared to twenty-twenty-five.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Beyond Ed, Anthropic, the company at the center of last week's lead story on federal model access, released a new research platform called Claude Science on June thirtieth, and Northeastern University researchers say it could accelerate their work, according to Northeastern Global News. Claude Science integrates more than sixty scientific databases and computation tools in a single workspace. Chemistry professor Jeffrey Agar, who studies protein changes in A.L.S., said an earlier Anthropic model transition brought improvement of nearly twenty percent in some areas of science. Researcher Michael Pollastri said automated information gathering could increase the pace of his lab's experimentation by orders of magnitude. A third faculty member, Jared Auclair, offered a cautious assessment, warning that general-purpose A.I. can produce errors on regulatory guidance or assay design, which carry real consequences in drug development. Auclair estimated that A.I. deployed well could compress drug development timelines from an average of ten to fifteen years down to two to five. Faculty also noted the beta currently runs only on Mac and Linux systems.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College is reporting a seven percent increase in fall enrollment, at a time when colleges nationally braced for declines tied to the demographic dip following the Great Recession, according to WLOX. President Mary Graham attributed the growth to deliberate recruitment shifts, including partnerships with district high schools that allow students to complete college coursework and potentially finish an associate's degree before graduating, along with outreach to adult learners and programs for military-connected students. The enrollment trend pairs with a workforce-training expansion anchored by the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network, a statewide initiative the college leads with partners including Intel, Dell, and Accelerate Mississippi. The college is also one of ten finalists, out of more than twelve hundred U.S. community colleges, for the Aspen Award, which carries a one-million-dollar prize. A decision is expected in April.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the research front, nearly one in five college students has turned to A.I. for mental health purposes, and students with severe symptoms are roughly twice as likely to do so, according to a study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders and co-authored by Fordham University psychology professor Tiffany Yip, as reported by Fordham Now. The study of six hundred seventy-five students found eighteen percent had used A.I. for mental health support, with rates roughly double among students with moderate or severe depression, severe anxiety, or suicidality. Using A.I. for everyday tasks like schoolwork or trip planning was among the strongest predictors of seeking mental health support from it. Yip warned that chatbots are designed to keep users engaged rather than to provide care, and are not meant to serve as mental health providers. The authors call for building crisis detection tools into chatbots and for educational outreach aimed at students most likely to seek A.I. support. A companion survey found students rate A.I. support as inferior to family, friends, and mental health professionals, though ratings rose when family support was less available.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. this week, an educational developer has proposed that colleges build what she calls human intelligence labs, staffed campus spaces where A.I. access is blocked so students can practice reading, writing, and problem-solving, according to a piece published in Inside Higher Ed. Author Karen Spira, an educational developer at a private liberal arts university and former tenure-stream Spanish professor, reports that by January twenty-twenty-six many faculty she coaches had stopped assigning essays because students were submitting A.I.-generated prose. Moving that work into class creates time pressure, she writes, since faculty typically see students for roughly one-third of expected learning time. The proposed labs would have trained staff monitor norms such as leaving devices in lockers. Spira distinguishes the concept from proctoring-centered testing centers, describing welcoming spaces designed to support practice rather than police assessment. The proposal weighs costs including space, staffing, accessibility planning, and e-textbook workarounds against what Spira cites as Big Tech's projected seven hundred billion dollars in A.I. spending in twenty-twenty-six.

<break time="1.0s"/>

West Texas A&M University researchers, faculty, and students now have access to VISION, ranked the most powerful university supercomputer in the United States and sixty-sixth among the world's fastest systems on the June twenty-twenty-six TOP500 list, through the university's membership in the Texas A&M University System, according to a West Texas A&M announcement. VISION features ninety-five computing nodes and seven hundred sixty graphics processing units and posted thirty-four point eight two petaflops of measured performance, part of a forty-five-million-dollar A&M System investment in advanced computing infrastructure. In one early drug-discovery project, Texas A&M researchers screened more than ten million compounds in about a week, work that would have taken years previously. Engineering dean Emily Hunt said access will enable larger A.I. models, accelerated simulations, and interdisciplinary projects beyond the university's local computing capacity.

<break time="1.0s"/>

California has approved its first new State Bar legal specialty in twenty years, a privacy law specialization, and the University of California, Berkeley School of Law has launched the first executive education program aligned with the credential, according to National Jurist. The Chief Privacy Officer Program, implemented by Berkeley Law Executive Education with the Berkeley Center for Law and Technology, launched in January and targets senior legal and privacy leaders navigating A.I. governance, tech regulation, and data compliance. It includes seven self-paced online modules and interactive sessions with Berkeley Law faculty and guest speakers. California and North Carolina are currently the only two states offering the certification.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Closing out this week's broadcast, nearly two hundred leaders from thirty higher education institutions gathered in Chicago this week to diagnose A.I. governance gaps and draft strategies to address them at Complete College America's AI and Student Success Summit, according to GovTech. Participants worked through a curriculum built on mission alignment, resource management, responsible data use, talent development, and change management. CCA President Yolanda Watson Spiva said A.I. is already reshaping the campus experience, often without governance, guardrails, or clear answers about who benefits. The summit extends CCA's A.I. Readiness Consortium, formed with Riipen, the same work-based learning platform featured in this week's Education Design Lab community-college story. CCA director of technology innovation Norm Palmer said A.I. in higher education is consistently framed as a technology adoption problem, but is better understood as an organizational design problem.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: Study of 21,559 Firms Finds Heaviest AI Adopters Grew Headcount 10.2 Percent
leadStory.summary: Companies that invested most heavily in A.I. hired more workers than those that invested little, according to new research from financial technology company Ramp and workforce intelligence firm Revelio Labs, USA Today reported. The researchers compared A.I. spending and employee data at 21,559 U.S. firms over a two-year period. 'Low-intensity' adopters, spending an average of $2.78 per employee on A.I., saw little change in headcount, while 'high-intensity' adopters spending an average of $33.67 per employee grew headcount by 10.2 percent — and entry-level headcount at those firms rose 12 percent, contradicting predictions that young or inexperienced workers face the greatest risk. The findings land amid anxiety: 53 percent of Americans worry A.I. could cost them or someone in their household a job, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released in June. Ramp Economics Lab lead economist Ara Kharazian cautioned that the sample skews toward tech-forward companies and white-collar roles, excluding drivers or manufacturing roles, and that headcounts could still change beyond the two-year window; the researchers stress the findings show correlation, not proof that A.I. spending causes hiring. Kharazian said the work matters because earlier research focused on A.I.-exposed industries and could not compare A.I. spending with staffing levels at the same firms. He noted that most firms using A.I. do not see results today; gains appear only after sustained, high-intensity use. Kory Kantenga, head of economics for the Americas at LinkedIn, said the hiring pattern makes sense: companies with money to spend on new technology also have money to spend on labor, growing A.I. startups need human resources, marketing, and sales staff, and new growth opportunities require more workers. Asked what he would tell a graduating job seeker, Kharazian said he would advise joining the company going all in on A.I. The research was also covered by NBC News.

quickHits.headline: Four Community Colleges Win Google-Backed Grants to Design AI-Ready Work-Based Learning
quickHits.summary: The Education Design Lab, in partnership with work-based learning platform Riipen and with support from Google.org, launched the AI + Durable Skills Work-Based Learning Design Challenge on July 1, selecting four community colleges to design work-based learning experiences that build students' A.I. fluency, the organization announced. The participating institutions are the Community College of Aurora in Colorado, Hudson County Community College in New Jersey, East Arkansas Community College, and Roxbury Community College in Boston. Each college receives a $10,000 implementation grant, access to Riipen's platform, and a facilitated design process led by the Lab. Pilot learning experiences launch in January 2027 and run through August 2027, with students completing employer-designed projects that reflect real-world A.I. use cases and receiving structured feedback from employers. The Lab said the colleges were selected for institutional readiness rather than interest in A.I. alone, and will publish an open-access library of tools, sample curricula, and best practices at the challenge's conclusion. The announcement cited research showing demand for A.I. literacy skills has grown more than 70 percent compared to 2025.

quickHits.headline: Northeastern Scientists Weigh Anthropic's New Claude Science Platform for Drug Discovery
quickHits.summary: Anthropic released Claude Science on June 30, a research platform integrating more than 60 scientific databases and computation tools in a single workspace — the company's answer to GPT-Rosalind, the research model OpenAI released in April — and Northeastern University researchers say it could accelerate their work, Northeastern Global News reported. Chemistry professor Jeffrey Agar, who studies protein changes in ALS, said he uses A.I. for hours daily and called Anthropic's earlier Sonnet-to-Opus model transition 'big for scientists,' with improvement of almost 20 percent in some areas of science. Michael Pollastri, who works on repurposing drugs for tropical diseases, said automated information gathering could increase the pace of his lab's experimentation 'by orders of magnitude.' Jared Auclair, who works in cell and gene therapy development, was cautiously optimistic, warning that general-purpose A.I. can hallucinate on regulatory guidance or assay design — errors that carry real consequences in drug development — while estimating that A.I. deployed well could compress drug development from 10 to 15 years on average to two to five. Faculty noted the beta currently runs only on Mac and Linux.

quickHits.headline: Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College Defies Enrollment Cliff With 7 Percent Fall Gain
quickHits.summary: Fall enrollment at Mississippi Gulf Coast Community College is up 7 percent — on top of a summer increase — at a time when colleges nationally braced for declines tied to the Great Recession-era dip in birth rates, WLOX reported. President Mary Graham attributed the growth to deliberate recruitment shifts: partnerships with district high schools that let students complete college work and potentially finish an associate's degree before graduating, outreach to adult learners, and programs for military-connected students. The enrollment trend pairs with a workforce-training expansion anchored by the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network, a statewide initiative MGCCC leads with partners including Intel, Dell, and Accelerate Mississippi, aimed at building a workforce that attracts A.I.-driven economic development to the state. MGCCC is also one of 10 finalists — out of more than 1,200 U.S. community colleges — for the Aspen Award, judged on outcomes, retention, transferability, and graduation rates, carrying a $1 million prize Graham said would fund scholarships or campus improvements. A decision is expected in April.

quickHits.headline: Study: Nearly One in Five College Students Uses AI for Mental Health Support
quickHits.summary: Nearly one in five college students has turned to A.I. for mental health purposes, and students with severe symptoms are roughly twice as likely to do so, according to a study co-authored by Fordham psychology professor Tiffany Yip and published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, Fordham Now reported. The study of 675 students at an art and design school and a large public university found 18 percent had used A.I. for mental health purposes, with rates roughly double among students with moderate or severe depression, severe anxiety, or suicidality. Using A.I. for everyday tasks like schoolwork or trip planning was among the strongest predictors of seeking mental health support from it. Yip warned that chatbots are programmed to keep people engaged rather than to provide care: 'They're not meant to be mental health providers.' In the paper, the authors call for building crisis detection tools into chatbots and for educational outreach aimed at students most likely to seek A.I. support. A companion survey of 92 Fordham undergraduates found students rate A.I. support as inferior to family, friends, and mental health professionals — but rated it higher when their families were less supportive.

quickHits.headline: As Take-Home Writing Collapses, an Educational Developer Proposes Staffed AI-Free 'Human Intelligence Labs'
quickHits.summary: Arguing that take-home writing assignments no longer measure student learning, a proposal published in Inside Higher Ed calls for colleges to build 'human intelligence labs' — staffed campus spaces where instructors can block A.I. access so students practice the reading, writing, and problem-solving skills of their disciplines. Author Karen Spira, an educational developer at a private liberal arts university and former tenure-stream Spanish professor, reports that by January 2026 many faculty she coaches had stopped assigning essays because students were submitting A.I.-generated prose, and math faculty found it untenable to grade homework outsourced to chatbots. Moving that work into class creates time scarcity, she writes, since faculty see students for roughly one-third of expected learning time. The design confronts the surveillance tension directly: trained staff would monitor norms such as leaving devices in lockers, but Spira distinguishes the labs from proctoring-centered testing centers, describing welcoming spaces that support practice rather than police assessment. Spira weighs the costs — space, staffing, accessibility planning, e-textbook workarounds — set against Big Tech's projected $700 billion A.I. spend in 2026.

quickHits.headline: West Texas A&M Gains Access to Nation's Fastest University Supercomputer
quickHits.summary: West Texas A&M University researchers, faculty, and students now have access to VISION, ranked the most powerful university supercomputer in the United States and No. 66 among the world's fastest systems on the June 2026 TOP500 list, through the university's membership in the Texas A&M University System, WTAMU announced. VISION, an NVIDIA DGX H200 SuperPOD housed at Texas A&M's West Campus Data Center, features 95 DGX nodes and 760 H200 graphics processing units and posted 34.82 petaflops of measured performance — part of a $45 million A&M System investment in advanced computing infrastructure. In one early drug-discovery project, Texas A&M researchers screened more than 10 million compounds in about a week, computing work that would have taken years in a previous environment. Engineering dean Emily Hunt said access will enable larger A.I. models, accelerated simulations, and interdisciplinary projects beyond WT's local computing capacity. WT earned Carnegie recognition as a Research College and University in 2025 and spends about $10 million annually on research.

quickHits.headline: California Approves First New State Bar Specialty in 20 Years; Berkeley Law Launches First Aligned Program
quickHits.summary: California has approved its first new State Bar legal specialty in 20 years — a privacy law specialization — and the University of California, Berkeley School of Law has launched the first executive education program aligned with the credential, National Jurist reported. The Chief Privacy Officer Program, implemented by Berkeley Law Executive Education with the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology, launched in January and targets senior legal and privacy leaders navigating A.I. governance, tech regulation, and data compliance. It includes seven self-paced online modules for working professionals and interactive sessions with Berkeley Law faculty and guest speakers; participants receive access to BCLT's B-CLE platform, including the content library needed to complete the remaining 60-hour education requirement for the specialization. Instructor Jeewon Serrato said the State Bar trustees' vote 'formally launches California's first Privacy Law Specialization, positioning the state at the forefront of a growing movement to recognize privacy law as a distinct, advanced discipline.' California and North Carolina are the only two states offering the certification.

quickHits.headline: Nearly 200 Higher Ed Leaders Draft AI Governance Strategies at Chicago Summit
quickHits.summary: Nearly 200 leaders from 30 higher education institutions spent two days in Chicago this week diagnosing their institutions' A.I. governance gaps and drafting strategies to close them at Complete College America's AI and Student Success Summit, GovTech reported. Participants worked through a curriculum built on mission alignment, resource management, responsible use of data and technology infrastructure, talent development, and change management — tenets outlined in a CCA report published in January 2025. CCA President Yolanda Watson Spiva said A.I. 'is already reshaping the campus experience, oftentimes without governance, guardrails or a clear answer to the most important questions — who benefits from it, and who gets left further behind?' The summit extends the nonprofit's AI Readiness Consortium, formed with work-based learning platform Riipen in 2025, and earlier case studies documenting a University of Louisiana A.I. microcredential, University of Massachusetts mini-grants for A.I. experimentation, and Arizona State University research challenges. 'AI in higher education is consistently framed as a technology adoption problem. It is not. It is an organizational design problem,' said Norm Palmer, CCA's director of technology innovation.
